Consent for Research Participation

Title

Using Adaptive Practice to Improve Recall and Understanding in Postsecondary Anatomy and Physiology

Sponsor

Department of Education, Institute of Educational Science

Researcher(s)

Philip Pavlik, University of Memphis

Andrew Olney, University of Memphis

Amanda Banker, Southwest Tennessee Community College

Researchers Contact Information

412-605-0581, ppavlik@memphis.edu

You are being asked to participate in a research study. The box below highlights key information for you to consider when deciding if you want to participate. More detailed information is provided below the box. Please ask the researcher(s) any questions about the study before you make your decision. If you volunteer, you will be one of about 75 people to do so.

Key Information for You to Consider

Voluntary Consent: You are being asked to volunteer for a research study. It is up to you whether you choose to participate or not. There will be no penalty or loss of benefit to which you are otherwise entitled if you choose not to participate or discontinue participation.

Purpose: The purpose of the study is to help us test an adaptive practice system for Anatomy and Physiology. You are being invited to participate because are a student in a participating section of Anatomy and Physiology at Southwest Tennessee Community College.

Duration: It is expected that your participation will last 3.5 hours, in 4 sessions, or more, depending on when you choose to do it.

Procedures and Activities : You will be asked to practice information in your text book for at least 3 hours on a computer or smartphone. The practice items will come from your textbook and are designed to help your long-term memory and understanding. There is a survey at the end that will take less than 30 minutes.

Risk: Some of the foreseeable risk or discomforts of your participation include boredom, wasted time if practice is ineffective, or stress if you find it difficult.

Benefits: Some of the benefits that may be expected include improved exam performance and data that allows us to improve the system for future classes.

Alternatives : If you do not want to take part in the study, as an alternative for each of the 3 chapters you will be able to submit a completed McGraw Hill study guide worksheet exercise that accompanies the textbook. Please see your instructor or syllabus for the details of the alternative. As a student if you decide not to take part in this study your choice will have no effect on your academic status or grade in your class.

Who is conducting this research?

Philip Pavlik of the University of Memphis, Institute of Intelligent Systems and Department of Psychology is in charge of the study. There may be other research team members assisting during the study.

What happens if I agree to participate in this Research?

If you agree you will be asked to you will sign-in sometime during the coursework for each exam and spend 3 hours practicing for each of 3 chapters of material. There are not different groups in this study, since we are in the process of improving the system before a comparison test. After the 3 hours of practice distributed with 1 hour on each of the 3 chapters of material, there will be brief survey that shouldn't take longer than 30 minutes, this survey is voluntary and not required for the extra credit, but lets you give feedback on the system to help us improve it. Practice itself is a sequence of fill-in-the blank items created from your textbook to maximize their relevance to the chapter material. You fill in the correct words using a practice app on your smartphone or computer. The items repeat until you learn them completely, which we expect will help in the course exams.

What happens to the information collected for this research?

By participating, you understand and agree that the deidentified data gathered during this study may be used by the University of Memphis and published and/or disclosed by the University of Memphis to others outside of the University of Memphis. However, no personally identifying information will ever be mentioned in any such publication or dissemination of the research data and/or results to other researchers. In fact, we will never receive any personally identifying information in the course of this study.

How will my privacy and data confidentiality be protected?

We are very careful to protect student's identity in the course of this research. Our data collection strategy is designed to never expose the true identity of students to our research team. Data-linkage will occur through a random login ID distributed to each student the first week of the course. Your instructors have been carefully informed that they should not share the identities of students with us, so we will only identify you with your assigned login. Only teachers will create the keys to match logins to individuals. We do not log GPS or IP address information. We will further deidentify your data (remove your ID) after the experiment before storing it on our password protected computers long-term.

What if I want to stop participating in this research?

It is up to you to decide whether you want to volunteer for this study. It is also ok to decide to end your participation at any time. There is no penalty or loss of benefits to which you are otherwise entitled if you decided to withdraw your participation. Your decision about participating will not affect your relationship with the researcher(s) or the University of Memphis or Southwest Tennessee Community College. You will receive partial credit for each hour of participation, i.e. 1% per hour.

Will it cost me money to take part in this research?

No.

Will I receive any compensation or reward for participating in this research?

For the 1 hour of practice on each of 3 chapters (total 3 hours) you will get 3% extra credit in the course.

Who can answer my question about this research?

Before you decide to volunteer for this study, if you have questions, suggestions, concerns, or complaints about the study, you can contact the investigator, Dr. Philip Pavlik at 412-605-0581 or email ppavlik@memphis.edu. If you have any questions about your rights as a volunteer in this research, contact the Institutional Review Board staff at the University of Memphis at 901-678-2705 or email irb@memphis.edu. You may print this screen webpage for your records.

By clicking below I am electronically signing, I volunteer to participate in this research. I understand that I am not waiving any legal rights. I may print a copy of this form.

Anatomy & Physiology Practice Instructions


Our MoFaCTS system has chosen some of the most important sentences from your textbook and they are presented here for your practice. This practice assumes you have read the textbook first, so that you understand the basic layout. For each sentence we remove keywords and the practice is to fill-in-the-blank for each sentence. Such quizzing has been proven to be an powerful aid to memory, and the system focuses on items you get wrong to make sure you learn all the items thouroughly. The system pronounces keywords to help you memorize them if you turn that on in the main menu. The system also provides the progress button above to check how much practice you have done, and how well our AI system thinks you have learned the words. We hope you will be able to use this progress information to decide if you want to continue the practice after you have completed the required amount.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels.First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

The Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen is a versatile element. It comes in many different chemical states. It has no color, odor, or taste. It can move through air, soil, and water. Nitrogen is a building block of life. Nature uses it to make DNA and proteins, and all plants need nitrogen to live and grow. The movement of nitrogen through the environment is called the nitrogen cycle. About 78% of the air we breathe is nitrogen gas. It comes from the atmosphere, but it can't be used by organisms in that form. This is because a strong chemical bond connects nitrogen atoms. Most plants can't use this atmospheric nitrogen because they can't break that bond. The bonded, inert nature of nitrogen gas makes all of it in the atmosphere seem useless. Fortunately, nature solved the problem. As you will see, nitrogen is abundant in ecosystems. Nitrogen cycles through ecosystems in five steps. These are nitrogen fixation, nitrogen uptake, nitrogen mineralization, nitrification, and denitrification. At each step, nitrogen chemically changes in what is called a nitrogen transformation. How this is accomplished is explained in the five steps below.

Nitrogen Fixation

The first step is nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is when organisms convert nitrogen gas to compounds usable by plants. These organisms are called nitrogen-fixers, and are usually bacteria. They don't break the strong chemical bond of nitrogen directly. Instead, they combine the nitrogen gas with hydrogen or oxygen, and form a new, usable compound. Soil bacteria from the genus Rhizobium do this. They take nitrogen from the air and convert it to ammonium by metabolic processes. Nitrogen is still in the ammonium, but it's changed its chemical form. In the ocean, blue-green algae are an important nitrogen fixer too. Natural events like lightning and lava flows also fix a little nitrogen by breaking the bonds of nitrogen atoms. Now free, the nitrogen can combine and form other compounds. Recently, humans have become an important source of fixed nitrogen. Burning fossil fuels, using nitrogen fertilizers, and growing legumes all fix nitrogen. In fact, humans now fix more nitrogen than all natural sources combined. This extra nitrogen can have bad effects on the environment. One example is with fertilizer, which is made from nitrogen. Humans grow crops with fertilizer. But if it rains, fertilizer may run off the farm and into rivers. The rivers take the fertilizer into the ocean where algae feed on the nitrogen in it. The algae bloom and suck oxygen out of the water. This forms what are called dead zones, and hundreds exist. Dead zones are terrible for fish and marine life.

Nitrogen Uptake

The second step is nitrogen uptake. Nitrogen uptake is the incorporation of fixed nitrogen, like ammonium, into a plant. Plants can absorb the nitrogen from the soil or from bacteria. In the soil, other bacteria have fixed nitrogen as ammonium or nitrate. Plants absorb this with their roots. It's the main way they get nitrogen. Plants use it to create their stems, leaves, and roots. But there is another way plants get nitrogen. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium often form symbiotic relationships with host plants. This symbiosis occurs in legumes (beans and peas). In this relationship, the legume lets nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in its roots and gives it food. In exchange, the plant gets some of the nitrogen the bacteria fix. Meanwhile, humans get their nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.

Nitrogen Mineralization

The third step is nitrogen mineralization. Mineralization is the conversion of organic nitrogen back to ammonium. Nitrogen occurs in two forms: inorganic (ammonium) and organic (stems, leaves, proteins). Plants can only use inorganic nitrogen as food. They use it to make leaves, stems, and roots and turn it into organic nitrogen. When plants die and decay, the organic nitrogen stored in leaves and stems can't be used by other plants. But it can be eaten and broken down back to inorganic nitrogen by bacteria and fungi. One example is a mushroom growing on a dead log. Organic nitrogen in the log's wood is turned back to an inorganic form like ammonium. That is mineralization in action. As ammonium, nitrogen can repeat this part of the cycle and be used by plants again. Or, it can change into nitrate by the step of nitrification.

Nitrification

The fourth step is nitrification. Nitrification is the conversion of ammonium to nitrate by bacteria. The bacteria gain energy from this reaction but need oxygen to do it. So, nitrification happens mostly in environments with more oxygen, like topsoil. But nitrate doesn't stick to soil easily when water's around. A heavy rain can wash nitrates into rivers or sink it deeper through soil into groundwater. Water carries around nitrate like a taxi cab. Too much nitrate in the groundwater is bad for human health. But for plants, nitrate is a great nutrient. It may end up in plant leaves if it's not washed away.

Denitrification

The final step is denitrification. Denitrification changes nitrate back into nitrogen gas and is done by denitrifying bacteria. These bacteria often live in swamps and lakes and need very little oxygen. It's almost the reverse of nitrogen fixation. Whereas fixation steals nitrogen from the air, denitrification gives it back. Once converted to nitrogen gas, the molecule escapes into the sky. Only denitrification removes nitrogen from ecosystems. It keeps nitrogen in balance. Without it, nitrogen compounds could build up to toxic levels in the soil. While helpful, denitrification can do harm. It makes nitric oxide and nitrous oxide gases. They cause smog, acid rain, and thin the ozone layer. However, humans have learned to harness denitrification. To clean water, water treatment plants have to remove the nitrates. To do this they pass the water through filters full of denitrifying bacteria. The bacteria change the nitrate to a gas and it leaves the water. The nitrogen cycle is one of nature's most elegant sleights-of-hand. It shuttles nitrogen from air to soil to plants and back again.

The Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen is a versatile element. It comes in many different chemical states. It has no color, odor, or taste. It can move through air, soil, and water. Nitrogen is a building block of life. Nature uses it to make DNA and proteins, and all plants need nitrogen to live and grow. The movement of nitrogen through the environment is called the nitrogen cycle. About 78% of the air we breathe is nitrogen gas. It comes from the atmosphere, but it can't be used by organisms in that form. This is because a strong chemical bond connects nitrogen atoms. Most plants can't use this atmospheric nitrogen because they can't break that bond. The bonded, inert nature of nitrogen gas makes all of it in the atmosphere seem useless. Fortunately, nature solved the problem. As you will see, nitrogen is abundant in ecosystems. Nitrogen cycles through ecosystems in five steps. These are nitrogen fixation, nitrogen uptake, nitrogen mineralization, nitrification, and denitrification. At each step, nitrogen chemically changes in what is called a nitrogen transformation. How this is accomplished is explained in the five steps below.

Nitrogen Fixation

The first step is nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is when organisms convert nitrogen gas to compounds usable by plants. These organisms are called nitrogen-fixers, and are usually bacteria. They don't break the strong chemical bond of nitrogen directly. Instead, they combine the nitrogen gas with hydrogen or oxygen, and form a new, usable compound. Soil bacteria from the genus Rhizobium do this. They take nitrogen from the air and convert it to ammonium by metabolic processes. Nitrogen is still in the ammonium, but it's changed its chemical form. In the ocean, blue-green algae are an important nitrogen fixer too. Natural events like lightning and lava flows also fix a little nitrogen by breaking the bonds of nitrogen atoms. Now free, the nitrogen can combine and form other compounds. Recently, humans have become an important source of fixed nitrogen. Burning fossil fuels, using nitrogen fertilizers, and growing legumes all fix nitrogen. In fact, humans now fix more nitrogen than all natural sources combined. This extra nitrogen can have bad effects on the environment. One example is with fertilizer, which is made from nitrogen. Humans grow crops with fertilizer. But if it rains, fertilizer may run off the farm and into rivers. The rivers take the fertilizer into the ocean where algae feed on the nitrogen in it. The algae bloom and suck oxygen out of the water. This forms what are called dead zones, and hundreds exist. Dead zones are terrible for fish and marine life.

Nitrogen Uptake

The second step is nitrogen uptake. Nitrogen uptake is the incorporation of fixed nitrogen, like ammonium, into a plant. Plants can absorb the nitrogen from the soil or from bacteria. In the soil, other bacteria have fixed nitrogen as ammonium or nitrate. Plants absorb this with their roots. It's the main way they get nitrogen. Plants use it to create their stems, leaves, and roots. But there is another way plants get nitrogen. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium often form symbiotic relationships with host plants. This symbiosis occurs in legumes (beans and peas). In this relationship, the legume lets nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in its roots and gives it food. In exchange, the plant gets some of the nitrogen the bacteria fix. Meanwhile, humans get their nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.

Nitrogen Mineralization

The third step is nitrogen mineralization. Mineralization is the conversion of organic nitrogen back to ammonium. Nitrogen occurs in two forms: inorganic (ammonium) and organic (stems, leaves, proteins). Plants can only use inorganic nitrogen as food. They use it to make leaves, stems, and roots and turn it into organic nitrogen. When plants die and decay, the organic nitrogen stored in leaves and stems can't be used by other plants. But it can be eaten and broken down back to inorganic nitrogen by bacteria and fungi. One example is a mushroom growing on a dead log. Organic nitrogen in the log's wood is turned back to an inorganic form like ammonium. That is mineralization in action. As ammonium, nitrogen can repeat this part of the cycle and be used by plants again. Or, it can change into nitrate by the step of nitrification.

Nitrification

The fourth step is nitrification. Nitrification is the conversion of ammonium to nitrate by bacteria. The bacteria gain energy from this reaction but need oxygen to do it. So, nitrification happens mostly in environments with more oxygen, like topsoil. But nitrate doesn't stick to soil easily when water's around. A heavy rain can wash nitrates into rivers or sink it deeper through soil into groundwater. Water carries around nitrate like a taxi cab. Too much nitrate in the groundwater is bad for human health. But for plants, nitrate is a great nutrient. It may end up in plant leaves if it's not washed away.

Denitrification

The final step is denitrification. Denitrification changes nitrate back into nitrogen gas and is done by denitrifying bacteria. These bacteria often live in swamps and lakes and need very little oxygen. It's almost the reverse of nitrogen fixation. Whereas fixation steals nitrogen from the air, denitrification gives it back. Once converted to nitrogen gas, the molecule escapes into the sky. Only denitrification removes nitrogen from ecosystems. It keeps nitrogen in balance. Without it, nitrogen compounds could build up to toxic levels in the soil. While helpful, denitrification can do harm. It makes nitric oxide and nitrous oxide gases. They cause smog, acid rain, and thin the ozone layer. However, humans have learned to harness denitrification. To clean water, water treatment plants have to remove the nitrates. To do this they pass the water through filters full of denitrifying bacteria. The bacteria change the nitrate to a gas and it leaves the water. The nitrogen cycle is one of nature's most elegant sleights-of-hand. It shuttles nitrogen from air to soil to plants and back again.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

What is Photosynthesis?

Plants need food but they do not have to wait on people or animals to provide for them. Most plants are autotrophs, able to make their own food whenever they need it. This is done using light and the process is called photosynthesis.

Before we go deeper into how photosynthesis works, let's sum it up. Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make their own food. To make food plants need carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight. Let's take a look at how these are collected by plants. Carbon dioxide from the air passes through small pores in the leaves. These pores are called stomata. Plants must guard against drying out and so have evolved stomata to allow gas to enter and leave the leaf. Water is absorbed by the roots and passes through vessels in the stem on its way to the leaves. Sunlight is absorbed by a green pigment in the leaves called chlorophyll.

Now that the necessary ingredients have been collected, the food can be made. Photosynthesis uses six molecules of water plus six molecules of carbon dioxide to make one molecule of sugar and six molecules of oxygen. After photosynthesis, the oxygen passes through pores in the leaf and into the air. The food is a sugar that stays behind in the plant.

Chlorophyll gives leaves their green color. Why is chlorophyll green? The answer has to do with wavelengths of light. White light which goes through a prism separates into different colors. These different colors are different wavelengths of light. Chlorophyll absorbs some of these wavelengths within the visible light spectrum, such as red (long wavelength) and blue (short wavelength) light. Green light is not absorbed but reflected by chlorophyll, making it appear green to our eyes.

Chlorophyll absorbs the sun's energy. This energy is used to split water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. That oxygen is released from the leaves into the atmosphere. Hydrogen and carbon dioxide are used to form glucose, also called sugar, the food for plants. Some of the glucose is used to provide energy for the growth and development of plants. The rest is stored in leaves, roots or fruits for later use by plants.

The Process of Photosynthesis

Now we will get into the finer details of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis takes place in the leaves of plants. The leaves are made up of very small cells. Inside these cells are tiny structures called chloroplasts. The chloroplast is like a small town that houses every structure needed for photosynthesis. In the chloroplasts are thylakoids, which are special membranes containing chlorophyll and where the photosynthesis reactions actually take place. Thylakoids are stacked like pancakes in stacks called grana.

Photosynthesis is a two-stage process. The first process is the light reactions, which requires the direct energy of light to make energy molecules for the second process, the dark reactions. The dark reactions can usually occur in the dark, if the energy molecules from the light reactions are present. The dark reactions use the products of the light reactions to form glucose.

In the light reactions, light strikes chlorophyll in such a way as to excite electrons to a higher energy state. In a series of reactions the energy is converted (along an electron transport process) into ATP and NADPH. ATP and NADPH are molecules which carry energy. The energy in ATP and NADPH is used to make glucose in the dark reactions. Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen ions in the process, releasing oxygen as a by-product of the reaction.

In the dark reactions, carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is captured. The carbon dioxide is combined with hydrogen to form glucose using the energy made from the light reactions. The incorporation of carbon dioxide into organic compounds is known as carbon fixation. Unlike the light reactions, the dark reactions take place outside the thylakoid and in the stroma. The stroma is a colorless fluid in the chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoid.

The glucose created by photosynthesis stores energy. Plants use that energy by breaking down the glucose in a process called respiration. In respiration, oxygen combines with glucose to produce carbon dioxide and water. The energy released by respiration gives plants energy for growing and repairing. The carbon dioxide and water from respiration escape through the pores in the leaf.

All living things release energy through respiration. Plants use oxygen during respiration just like animals. Plants produce more oxygen than carbon dioxide because plants don't always use oxygen to break down glucose for energy. Glucose is soluble and moves throughout the plant. Most glucose is converted into building blocks like cellulose that make up the plant's body. But some glucose is also converted to insoluble starch, which stays inside cells. Starch can be turned back into glucose when it's needed for energy.

Implications of Photosynthesis

Some of the glucose that plants produce during photosynthesis is stored in fruits and roots. This is why we are able to eat carrots, potatoes, apples, water melons and all the others. These foods provide energy for humans and animals.

Oxygen that is produced during photosynthesis is released into the atmosphere. This oxygen is what we breathe and we cannot live without it. While it is important that photosynthesis provides food and oxygen, its impact on our daily lives is far more extensive. All of our energy for growth, development and physical activity comes from eating food from plants and animals. Animals obtain energy from eating plants. Plants obtain energy from glucose made during photosynthesis.

Our major sources of energy such as natural gas, coal, and oil were made millions of years ago from the remains of dead plants and animals which we already know got their energy from photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is also responsible for balancing oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere. Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen during the process of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is so essential to life on earth that most living organisms, including humans, cannot survive without it.

The Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen is a versatile element. It comes in many different chemical states. It has no color, odor, or taste. It can move through air, soil, and water. Nitrogen is a building block of life. Nature uses it to make DNA and proteins, and all plants need nitrogen to live and grow. The movement of nitrogen through the environment is called the nitrogen cycle. About 78% of the air we breathe is nitrogen gas. It comes from the atmosphere, but it can't be used by organisms in that form. This is because a strong chemical bond connects nitrogen atoms. Most plants can't use this atmospheric nitrogen because they can't break that bond. The bonded, inert nature of nitrogen gas makes all of it in the atmosphere seem useless. Fortunately, nature solved the problem. As you will see, nitrogen is abundant in ecosystems. Nitrogen cycles through ecosystems in five steps. These are nitrogen fixation, nitrogen uptake, nitrogen mineralization, nitrification, and denitrification. At each step, nitrogen chemically changes in what is called a nitrogen transformation. How this is accomplished is explained in the five steps below.

Nitrogen Fixation

The first step is nitrogen fixation. Nitrogen fixation is when organisms convert nitrogen gas to compounds usable by plants. These organisms are called nitrogen-fixers, and are usually bacteria. They don't break the strong chemical bond of nitrogen directly. Instead, they combine the nitrogen gas with hydrogen or oxygen, and form a new, usable compound. Soil bacteria from the genus Rhizobium do this. They take nitrogen from the air and convert it to ammonium by metabolic processes. Nitrogen is still in the ammonium, but it's changed its chemical form. In the ocean, blue-green algae are an important nitrogen fixer too. Natural events like lightning and lava flows also fix a little nitrogen by breaking the bonds of nitrogen atoms. Now free, the nitrogen can combine and form other compounds. Recently, humans have become an important source of fixed nitrogen. Burning fossil fuels, using nitrogen fertilizers, and growing legumes all fix nitrogen. In fact, humans now fix more nitrogen than all natural sources combined. This extra nitrogen can have bad effects on the environment. One example is with fertilizer, which is made from nitrogen. Humans grow crops with fertilizer. But if it rains, fertilizer may run off the farm and into rivers. The rivers take the fertilizer into the ocean where algae feed on the nitrogen in it. The algae bloom and suck oxygen out of the water. This forms what are called dead zones, and hundreds exist. Dead zones are terrible for fish and marine life.

Nitrogen Uptake

The second step is nitrogen uptake. Nitrogen uptake is the incorporation of fixed nitrogen, like ammonium, into a plant. Plants can absorb the nitrogen from the soil or from bacteria. In the soil, other bacteria have fixed nitrogen as ammonium or nitrate. Plants absorb this with their roots. It's the main way they get nitrogen. Plants use it to create their stems, leaves, and roots. But there is another way plants get nitrogen. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria like Rhizobium often form symbiotic relationships with host plants. This symbiosis occurs in legumes (beans and peas). In this relationship, the legume lets nitrogen-fixing bacteria live in its roots and gives it food. In exchange, the plant gets some of the nitrogen the bacteria fix. Meanwhile, humans get their nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.

Nitrogen Mineralization

The third step is nitrogen mineralization. Mineralization is the conversion of organic nitrogen back to ammonium. Nitrogen occurs in two forms: inorganic (ammonium) and organic (stems, leaves, proteins). Plants can only use inorganic nitrogen as food. They use it to make leaves, stems, and roots and turn it into organic nitrogen. When plants die and decay, the organic nitrogen stored in leaves and stems can't be used by other plants. But it can be eaten and broken down back to inorganic nitrogen by bacteria and fungi. One example is a mushroom growing on a dead log. Organic nitrogen in the log's wood is turned back to an inorganic form like ammonium. That is mineralization in action. As ammonium, nitrogen can repeat this part of the cycle and be used by plants again. Or, it can change into nitrate by the step of nitrification.

Nitrification

The fourth step is nitrification. Nitrification is the conversion of ammonium to nitrate by bacteria. The bacteria gain energy from this reaction but need oxygen to do it. So, nitrification happens mostly in environments with more oxygen, like topsoil. But nitrate doesn't stick to soil easily when water's around. A heavy rain can wash nitrates into rivers or sink it deeper through soil into groundwater. Water carries around nitrate like a taxi cab. Too much nitrate in the groundwater is bad for human health. But for plants, nitrate is a great nutrient. It may end up in plant leaves if it's not washed away.

Denitrification

The final step is denitrification. Denitrification changes nitrate back into nitrogen gas and is done by denitrifying bacteria. These bacteria often live in swamps and lakes and need very little oxygen. It's almost the reverse of nitrogen fixation. Whereas fixation steals nitrogen from the air, denitrification gives it back. Once converted to nitrogen gas, the molecule escapes into the sky. Only denitrification removes nitrogen from ecosystems. It keeps nitrogen in balance. Without it, nitrogen compounds could build up to toxic levels in the soil. While helpful, denitrification can do harm. It makes nitric oxide and nitrous oxide gases. They cause smog, acid rain, and thin the ozone layer. However, humans have learned to harness denitrification. To clean water, water treatment plants have to remove the nitrates. To do this they pass the water through filters full of denitrifying bacteria. The bacteria change the nitrate to a gas and it leaves the water. The nitrogen cycle is one of nature's most elegant sleights-of-hand. It shuttles nitrogen from air to soil to plants and back again.

Hallucinations occur when someone experiences sensations that actually do not exist, such as hearing voices coming from the mailbox.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels.First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Operational definitions are an exact set of procedures used to represent a particular concept.

Gestalt psychologists studied thinking, learning, and perception in whole units, as opposed to analyzing these experiences in smaller units.

Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalytic psychology, believed that our unconscious thoughts, impulses, and desires strongly influenced our behaviors.

Psychiatrists are medical doctors who treat psychological disorders with medication.

Experiments require a researchers to create two groups (a control group and an experimental group), vary a condition among the groups, and record data of the effects in each condition.

Dependent variables measure results of an experiment and are directly affected by the independent variables. Dependent variable are often revealed by measures of performance.

Random assignment of participants to each condition within an experiment can be used to minimize effects of extraneous variables that might unintentionally affect the outcome of the experiment.

The control group and the experimental group in an experiment are treated exactly the same except for the independent variable.

Placebos are often given to participants within the control group to make them believe they have been given the drug, or the true independent variable.

In a single-blind study, participants are unaware of who is in the experimental group and who is in the control group, but the experimenters do know the members of each group.

A double-blind experiment is one in which neither the participants, nor the experimenters, are aware of who is in the experimental group and who is in the control group.

The observer effect states that participants may change their behaviors when they are aware that they are being watched.

A negative correlation is one in which a decrease in one measure is matched with an increase in another measure. The measures will always move in the opposite direction of each other.

A positive correlation is one in which a decrease or increase in one measure is matched with a movement in the same direction in the other measure. The measures will always move in the same direction as each other.

Events that occur immediately before the response are called antecedents.

Linking a neutral antecedent stimulus with a stimulus that does produces an involuntary response is called classical conditioning.

Classical conditioning is based on the antecedents, or what happens before a behavior or response. An antecedent is called a stimulus when it is used during classical conditioning.

Shaping is the gradual molding of responses to a desired pattern of behavior(s).

Negative reinforcements increase the probability of repeating a response.

Punishments are events that follow responses and decrease the likelihood of that response occurring again.

Token economies use secondary, token, reinforcers to provide positive reinforcement after a behavior. These tokens can then later be exchanged for primary reinforcers.

Variable ratio schedules of reinforcement present a reinforcement after an unpredictable amount of time and are the most resistant to extinction.

Out of the three tools used to control behavior (nonreinforcement, reinforcement, and punishment), it is usually best to use positive reinforcement.

The three basic processes of memory are encoding, storage, and retrieval.

Encoding is the process of memory in which sensory information is converted into a form that can be stored in memory.

Storage is the process of memory in which encoded information is held for later use.

Chunking involves grouping bits of information into larger units as a way to improve the efficiency of short-term memory.

Elaborative processing involves linking new information to previously encoded and stored knowledge and memories, and is the most effective way to transfer short-term memories into long-term storage.

Spreading activation refers to reconstructing memories by starting with one recollection and following chains of associations to other related memories.

The serial position effect says that you are most likely to forget the middle items on a list while remembering the first and last items on that list.

Sequential lineups are ones in which a witness is shown one photo at a time.

State dependent learning refers to the fact that bodily states and moods can be encoded and stored as part of a memory, and therefore be a strong cue for later recall of that memory.

Sleeping after studying can increase memory because there is less interference during sleep.

Interference is the tendency for new memories to get in the way of recalling old memories, or for old memories to get in the way of recalling new memories.

Consolidation is the formation of long-term memories in the brain.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.

The Circulatory System

The Heart

An adult's heart is about the size of a large orange and weighs a little less than a pound. It is hollow and can fill up with blood. The heart is in the middle of the chest. It fits snugly between the two lungs. The pointed tip at the bottom of the heart touches the front wall of the chest. Every time the heart beats, it goes 'thump' against the chest wall.

The heart is a pump. Its walls are made of thick muscle. They can squeeze (contract) to send blood rushing out. The blood flows smoothly in tubes called blood vessels. First the blood flows into tubes called arteries. The arteries that leave the heart are thick tubes. But the arteries soon branch again and again, to form many smaller tubes. These blood vessels carry blood to all parts of the body.

The farther from the heart, the more blood vessels there are. The tiniest blood vessels, called capillaries, are so small you would need a microscope to see them. Capillaries join to form larger blood vessels. These tubes carry blood back toward the heart. The bigger ones are called veins. The closer to the heart, the fewer the veins there are, and the larger they are. Therefore, the blood vessels carry blood in a circle. First moving away from the heart in the arteries, then traveling to various parts of the body in capillaries, and lastly going back to the heart through the veins.

If you could see inside your heart you would see that a vertical wall of (solid) muscle divides it down the middle, into a left half and a right half. The muscular wall is called a septum. Another septum in the heart is horizontal and separates the rounded top part of the heart from the cone-shaped bottom part. So there are actually four chambers (spaces) inside the heart. Each top chamber is called an atrium (plural: atria) and can be thought of as "receiving" chambers. The bottom chambers are called ventricles and can be thought of as "discharging" chambers. Blood can flow from the atria down into the ventricles, because there are openings in the horizontal septum that separates them. But the vertical septum is solid, with no openings.

The Circulation of Blood

The circulatory system is actually made up of two circles. The heart is a double pump whose two parts work in unison. The right side receives the blood from veins and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives the blood from the lungs and pumps it to the rest of the body. Blood cannot flow back and forth between the left and right halves of the heart, because the septum that separates them is solid, keeping the two circles separate.

The left ventricle of the heart sends blood out through a big artery and from there, into branching arteries that carry it to various parts of the body. The veins that carry blood back from the body parts empty the blood into the right atrium of the heart. The blood then flows down into the right ventricle, which pumps it into the lungs and back to the heart, into the left atrium. From there the blood flows into the left ventricle, where it is once again pumped out into the body.

All the cells of the body need energy to do their work. They get energy by combining sugars or other food materials with oxygen. When a body cell combines sugar with oxygen to get energy, carbon dioxide is formed. But too much carbon dioxide could poison a cell. So, all the body cells need some way to get oxygen and some way to get rid of carbon dioxide.

The blood does both these things. It brings oxygen to the body cells and takes away their carbon dioxide. These gases pass easily back and forth through the thin walls of the tiny capillaries. Both oxygen and carbon dioxide are carried in the blood mainly by the red blood cells. These tiny cells are like little ferry boats. They float along in the blood, carrying their cargoes of oxygen or carbon dioxide. As the blood flows through the capillaries in the body, carrying its supply of oxygen, it also collects carbon dioxide. The blood is then returned to the right atrium. The blood is then pumped into the right ventricle, and then to the lungs.

Inside the lungs there are many tiny air sacs called alveoli. They are wrapped in a network of tiny capillaries. Blood from the heart flows through these capillaries, passing carbon dioxide into the tiny air sacs. When you breathe out, you get rid of this carbon dioxide. Oxygen from the air sacs, obtained from breathing in, then passes into the blood capillaries. The oxygen-rich blood is returned to the left atrium of the heart and pumped out to the body through the left ventricle. Thus, the circle begins again. Even though it is the same blood that carried the carbon dioxide wastes, it has now unloaded them and taken on a new cargo of oxygen.

The Heartbeat

A heartbeat has two parts. First the heart muscle contracts. The contraction starts with the atria, which push blood into the ventricles. Then the walls of the ventricles squeeze together and force the blood out into the arteries. The contraction is the first part of the heartbeat. After that, the heart muscle relaxes, which is the second part of the heartbeat. This allows the heart to get large again, and blood can flow into the atria from the veins.

Blood cannot flow backward into the arteries because little trapdoors called valves stop it. Valves also guard the openings from the atria into the ventricles. So there is always one-way traffic in the heart. The valves keep blood from flowing backward. These valves, and every other component discussed in this text, are essential in maintaining a healthy heart and normal blood circulation.
